notes: Two identity/spelling flags carried in this file, per methodology rule 7: (1) Psalm 34's superscription names the king "Abimelech," while the episode it recalls (1 Samuel 21:10-15) names him "Achish king of Gath" — likely "Abimelech" functioned as a dynastic title for Philistine kings (as with the separate Abimelechs of Genesis 20 and 26), not a personal name; flagged under David rather than silently reconciled. This is distinct from "Ahimelech" the priest of Nob named in Psalm 52's superscription (1 Samuel 21-22) — two different names, easily confused, kept separate here. (2) "The Ezrahite" title is shared by two psalmists, Heman (Psalm 88) and Ethan (Psalm 89); both may or may not be the same individuals listed among Solomon's wise-men comparisons in 1 Kings 4:31 and the "sons of Zerah" genealogy of 1 Chronicles 2:6, and/or the Levitical musicians of 1 Chronicles 6:33 and 15:17-19 — scripture does not resolve this, and neither identification is asserted as certain in either entry. Genealogies for figures whose full family record belongs to other narrative books (David, Solomon, Moses) are kept minimal here and point back to those books rather than re-deriving full family trees within a poetry book that does not itself narrate them. Redraft supersedes the prior first-draft version: it adds standalone coverage for Psalm 89 (the Davidic Covenant psalm, via a new Ethan the Ezrahite manager entry) and promotes Heman the Ezrahite out of a bulk genealogyLists entry into a fully written "named" character, since he holds an individual authorial credit on Psalm 88.

characters.name: The Five Books of the Psalms
characters.deliveredBy: Compiled from many psalmists — David, Asaph, the sons of Korah, Solomon, Moses, Heman, Ethan, and numerous anonymous writers
characters.purpose: The Psalter is organized into five books (1-41, 42-72, 73-89, 90-106, 107-150), each closing with a doxology, mirroring the five books of the Torah — framing Israel's whole worship-book as a structured response to God's law.

verses.note: Opening gateway psalm, itself untitled: 'Blessed is the man...his delight is in the law of the LORD' — sets the frame for the entire Psalter before any author is named.
Doxology closing Book I: 'Blessed be the LORD God of Israel from everlasting, and to everlasting. Amen, and Amen.'
Doxology closing Book II, immediately after Solomon's psalm.
Doxology closing Book III, immediately after Ethan the Ezrahite's covenant psalm.
Doxology closing Book IV.
Final verse of Book V and of the whole Psalter: 'Let every thing that hath breath praise the LORD.'

funFacts: The five-book division is ancient, reflected in the Masoretic Text itself, not a later editorial addition.
Psalms 1 and 2 carry no author's name in their titles and together function as a twin gateway to the whole book.

characters.name: Royal & Messianic Psalms
characters.deliveredBy: David (Psalms 2, 110), the sons of Korah (Psalm 45), Solomon (Psalm 72)
characters.purpose: A recurring cluster of psalms written for or about Israel's anointed king, read by New Testament writers as pointing beyond any earthly king to the Messiah.

verses.note: 'Thou art my Son; this day have I begotten thee' — quoted of Jesus at His baptism and transfiguration (Matthew 3:17) and in Acts 13:33, Hebrews 1:5.
'My God, my God, why hast thou forsaken me?' — quoted by Jesus on the cross (Matthew 27:46).
Royal wedding psalm addressed to the king; quoted of Christ in Hebrews 1:8.
Solomon's coronation psalm: 'He shall have dominion also from sea to sea.'
'The LORD said unto my Lord, Sit thou at my right hand' — David's own psalm about a superior 'Lord'; Jesus cites it in Matthew 22:41-45 to question the scribes on the Messiah's identity.

funFacts: Psalm 110 is the single most-quoted Old Testament chapter in the New Testament.
Psalm 89 (the Davidic Covenant psalm, by Ethan the Ezrahite) is closely related in theme to this cluster but is substantial enough to warrant its own dedicated coverage — see Ethan the Ezrahite.

characters.name: David

children: and others named in 2 Samuel / 1 Chronicles
genealogy.note: David's full family record is documented in 1-2 Samuel and 1 Chronicles; only the relations his own psalm superscriptions reference are detailed here.

verses.note: Superscription: 'A Psalm of David, when he fled from Absalom his son' — set during the rebellion narrated in 2 Samuel 15-18.
Superscription names 'the words of Cush the Benjamite' as the psalm's occasion — Cush is not otherwise identified anywhere in the historical books.
Superscription: written 'in the day that the LORD delivered him from the hand of all his enemies, and from the hand of Saul' — near-identical text also appears in 2 Samuel 22.
'The LORD is my shepherd; I shall not want' — the single most memorized psalm in the Psalter; see its own dedicated entry.

Superscription names the king as 'Abimelech,' but the episode it recalls (1 Samuel 21:10-15) names him 'Achish king of Gath' — likely 'Abimelech' functioned as a royal title for Philistine kings (as in Genesis 20, 26), not a personal name; flagged as a real naming variance, not silently resolved.
Superscription: written 'when Nathan the prophet came unto him, after he had gone in to Bath-sheba' — the confrontation is narrated in 2 Samuel 12.

Superscription: 'when Doeg the Edomite came and told Saul... David is come to the house of Ahimelech' — the massacre at Nob follows in 1 Samuel 22. Note: 'Ahimelech' the priest here is a different name from 'Abimelech' in the Psalm 34 title above.
Superscription: 'when the Ziphims came and said to Saul, Doth not David hide himself with us?' — reported in 1 Samuel 23:19 and 26:1.
'Bless the LORD, O my soul' — one of David's best-known hymns of praise.
'I am fearfully and wonderfully made' — meditation on God's intimate knowledge of the psalmist.

funFacts: Credited as author in the superscriptions of at least 73 of the 150 psalms — more than any other named contributor.
Called 'the sweet psalmist of Israel' in 2 Samuel 23:1.
Several of David's psalm superscriptions (notably Psalm 18) closely parallel prose passages in 2 Samuel, preserving the same events in both narrative and poetic form.

characters.name: Psalm 23 — The Shepherd Psalm
characters.purpose: A short psalm of trust portraying the LORD as a shepherd who provides, guides, and protects, and as a host who welcomes the psalmist to a table even 'in the presence of mine enemies' — likely the single most widely memorized passage in the entire Bible, central to this game's mission.

verses.note: 'The LORD is my shepherd; I shall not want.'
'Yea, though I walk through the valley of the shadow of death, I will fear no evil: for thou art with me.'
'Surely goodness and mercy shall follow me all the days of my life: and I will dwell in the house of the LORD for ever.'

funFacts: Only six verses long, yet consistently ranked among the most quoted and memorized chapters of the entire Bible.
Attributed to David, whose own early life as a literal shepherd (1 Samuel 16:11) likely shaped its imagery.

characters.name: Imprecatory Psalms
characters.purpose: A recurring category of psalms in which the psalmist openly asks God to judge and punish enemies — raw, unfiltered prayers of lament and appeal to divine justice rather than an endorsement of personal vengeance.

verses.note: 'Plead my cause, O LORD, with them that strive with me.'
'The zeal of thine house hath eaten me up' — quoted of Jesus in John 2:17.
Quoted in Acts 1:20 regarding Judas Iscariot's replacement among the apostles.
'By the rivers of Babylon, there we sat down, yea, we wept, when we remembered Zion' — written out of the Babylonian exile; carries no author's name in its own text.

funFacts: Psalm 137 has no superscription naming an author, yet is placed within Book V among David's and Solomon's psalms.
Psalm 109:8 is directly quoted in the New Testament in Acts 1:20.

characters.name: The Sons of Korah

genealogy.note: A Levitical musical guild descended from Korah, whose own rebellion against Moses is narrated in Numbers 16. Scripture states Korah's own sons did not die with him (Numbers 26:11), and their line became temple singers and gatekeepers under David (1 Chronicles 6:31-38, 9:19).

verses.note: 'As the hart panteth after the water brooks, so panteth my soul after thee, O God' — opens Book II under this guild's name.
'God is our refuge and strength, a very present help in trouble.'
'How amiable are thy tabernacles, O LORD of hosts!... My soul longeth, yea, even fainteth for the courts of the LORD.'
Praise of Zion, 'the city of God.'
Superscription credits this psalm jointly 'for the sons of Korah' and 'of Heman the Ezrahite' — the Psalter's bleakest psalm, ending without resolution; see Heman the Ezrahite for the co-author.

funFacts: Ten psalms bear this guild's name in their superscriptions (42, 44-49, 84, 85, 87, and jointly 88).
The KJV superscriptions themselves say 'for the sons of Korah,' naming a family/guild rather than any one individual author.

characters.name: Heman the Ezrahite

genealogy.note: Named in Psalm 88's superscription as co-author alongside 'the sons of Korah.' His identity is genuinely uncertain: he may be the 'Heman' listed among the wise men of 1 Kings 4:31 (a son of Zerah, per 1 Chronicles 2:6, hence 'the Ezrahite' — of Zerah), or he may be Heman the Levite singer and grandson of Samuel appointed by David in 1 Chronicles 6:33 and 15:17. Scripture does not resolve which, and neither identification is asserted as certain here.

verses.note: Superscription: 'A Song or Psalm for the sons of Korah, to the chief Musician upon Mahalath Leannoth, Maschil of Heman the Ezrahite.'
The psalm's final verse: 'Lover and friend hast thou put far from me, and mine acquaintance into darkness' — Psalm 88 is unique in the Psalter for ending on unrelieved lament with no turn to praise.

funFacts: Psalm 88 is widely noted as the darkest psalm in the Psalter — it opens in distress and never resolves into praise or hope by its final verse.

Heman is one of only two psalmists in the Psalter given the title 'the Ezrahite,' the other being Ethan the Ezrahite (Psalm 89) — the two names appear together in the same genealogical list at 1 Chronicles 2:6.

characters.name: Asaph

genealogy.note: A Levite appointed by David as one of the chief temple musicians alongside Heman and Jeduthun (1 Chronicles 16:5, 25:1); his descendants ('the sons of Asaph') continued as a guild of temple singers for generations (1 Chronicles 25:2, Ezra 2:41).

verses.note: Opens with a vivid courtroom scene of God summoning the earth to judgment.
'Truly God is good to Israel... But as for me, my feet were almost gone' — a wisdom psalm wrestling with the prosperity of the wicked.

A national lament describing the sanctuary burned and desecrated (74:3-8); its severity has led many readers to associate it with Babylon's destruction of Solomon's temple, generations after the historical Asaph — the psalm's own text does not date the event, and 'Asaph' may here represent the ongoing Asaphite musical guild (1 Chronicles 25:1-2) rather than the individual personally.
A long historical psalm recounting Israel's history from the Exodus onward, meant to be taught to future generations.
A national lament naming a coalition of hostile neighboring nations.

funFacts: Twelve psalms (50, 73-83) bear Asaph's name — the largest block after David's.
1 Chronicles 16:5 records that Asaph was appointed 'to sound with cymbals' at the ark's installation under David.

characters.name: Solomon

spouses: numerous wives and concubines, detailed in 1 Kings 11
genealogy.note: Son of David and Bath-sheba (2 Samuel 12:24); full reign, wisdom, and family detail is covered in 1 Kings and 2 Chronicles — noted here only for the two psalms his superscriptions credit to him.

verses.note: 'Give the king thy judgments, O God, and thy righteousness unto the king's son' — a coronation prayer, closing Book II.
'Except the LORD build the house, they labour in vain that build it' — a wisdom psalm on the futility of labor without God.

funFacts: Only two psalms (72 and 127) are attributed to Solomon, far fewer than the songs and proverbs 1 Kings 4:32 credits him with composing overall.
Psalm 72's closing line, 'The prayers of David the son of Jesse are ended' (72:20), marks a literary seam in the Psalter even though psalms attributed to David continue to appear later in the book.

characters.name: Ethan the Ezrahite

genealogy.note: Named in Psalm 89's superscription. Possibly the same 'Ethan the Ezrahite' listed among the wise men Solomon surpassed in 1 Kings 4:31, and among 'the sons of Zerah' in 1 Chronicles 2:6 (hence 'the Ezrahite'); scripture does not confirm this is the same individual as the Levite musician of the same name in 1 Chronicles 15:17,19. Neither identification is asserted as certain here.

verses.note: 'I will sing of the mercies of the LORD for ever' — opens the psalm that closes Book III.

'I have made a covenant with my chosen, I have sworn unto David my servant, Thy seed will I establish for ever, and build up thy throne to all generations' — the Davidic Covenant stated in the psalm's own words.
'My covenant will I not break, nor alter the thing that is gone out of my lips.'

A sudden, sobering turn: 'But thou hast cast off and abhorred, thou hast been wroth with thine anointed... thou hast made void the covenant of thy servant' — the psalm laments an apparent breach of the very covenant it just celebrated, likely written after a national defeat.
Closing doxology of Book III: 'Blessed be the LORD for evermore. Amen, and Amen.'

funFacts: Psalm 89 is one of the Old Testament's clearest statements of the Davidic Covenant — God's promise that David's throne would endure forever, later understood as fulfilled in Christ (Luke 1:32-33).

The psalm's dramatic shift from confident praise (verses 1-37) to anguished complaint (verses 38-51) makes it one of the Psalter's most theologically striking single chapters, and it closes Book III of the Psalms.
Ethan is one of only two psalmists given the title 'the Ezrahite,' the other being Heman (Psalm 88) — see Heman the Ezrahite for the shared identification question.

characters.name: Moses

genealogy.note: Full life narrated across Exodus through Deuteronomy; noted here only for his one credited psalm.

verses.note: 'Lord, thou hast been our dwelling place in all generations... from everlasting to everlasting, thou art God.'
'The days of our years are threescore years and ten... yet is their strength labour and sorrow.'
'So teach us to number our days, that we may apply our hearts unto wisdom.'

funFacts: Psalm 90 is the only psalm in the entire Psalter credited to Moses, and by internal dating is generally regarded as the oldest psalm in the collection.
It opens Book IV of the Psalter, immediately after the anguished close of Psalm 89.

characters.name: Psalm 119 — The Great Acrostic
characters.purpose: A sustained, 176-verse meditation praising and pleading for devotion to God's law, word, statutes, and commandments — structured as an acrostic with 22 eight-verse stanzas, one per letter of the Hebrew alphabet.

verses.note: 'Blessed are the undefiled in the way, who walk in the law of the LORD.'
'Thy word have I hid in mine heart, that I might not sin against thee.'
'Thy word is a lamp unto my feet, and a light unto my path.'
Final verse, ending in humble admission rather than triumph: 'I have gone astray like a lost sheep; seek thy servant.'

funFacts: The longest chapter in the entire Bible, at 176 verses.
No author is named in its superscription — it is untitled in the Hebrew text.

characters.name: Songs of Ascent
characters.deliveredBy: David (Psalms 122, 124, 131, 133), Solomon (Psalm 127), and anonymous psalmists for the remainder
characters.purpose: A collection of fifteen short psalms (120-134), each titled 'A Song of degrees,' traditionally understood as pilgrim songs sung while going up to Jerusalem for Israel's annual feasts.

verses.note: Opens the collection: 'In my distress I cried unto the LORD, and he heard me.'
'I will lift up mine eyes unto the hills, from whence cometh my help. My help cometh from the LORD.'
David's psalm: 'I was glad when they said unto me, Let us go into the house of the LORD.'
David's psalm: 'Behold, how good and how pleasant it is for brethren to dwell together in unity!'
Closes the collection with a call to bless the LORD.

funFacts: Four of the fifteen are credited to David and one to Solomon; the rest carry no named author.
The Hebrew title has also been read as 'Songs of the Steps,' a phrase later Jewish tradition tied to the temple's steps.

characters.name: The Closing Hallel
characters.purpose: The Psalter's final five psalms (146-150), each opening and closing with 'Praise ye the LORD' (Hallelujah), building to a crescendo of praise that closes the entire book.

verses.note: 'Praise ye the LORD... While I live will I praise the LORD.'
Calls sun, moon, stars, and 'ye heavens of heavens' to praise God.
'Praise ye the LORD. Praise God in his sanctuary.'
Final verse of the entire Psalter: 'Let every thing that hath breath praise the LORD. Praise ye the LORD.'

funFacts: None of these five closing psalms carries any author's name in its superscription.
Psalm 150 names essentially every instrument used in temple worship — trumpet, psaltery, harp, timbrel, stringed instruments, organs, and cymbals — in its final call to praise.

characters.name: Jeduthun
characters.perkNote: Chief musician credited in the superscriptions of both Davidic and Asaphite psalms — a worship-leading boost tied to David's tier.

genealogy.note: Named as one of David's three chief musicians in 1 Chronicles 16:41-42 and 25:1, alongside Asaph and Heman; his descendants continued as temple musicians (1 Chronicles 25:3).

verses.note: Superscription: 'To the chief Musician, even to Jeduthun, A Psalm of David.'
Superscription: 'To the chief Musician, to Jeduthun, A Psalm of David.'

Superscription: 'To the chief Musician, to Jeduthun, A Psalm of Asaph' — Jeduthun's name appears on an Asaph psalm as well as David's, reflecting a shared musical-director role rather than exclusive attachment to either author.

funFacts: Jeduthun is named in three psalm superscriptions total — two of David's and one of Asaph's.
1 Chronicles 25:3 lists his sons as prophesying 'with a harp, to give thanks and to praise the LORD.'

characters.name: Nathan the Prophet
characters.perkNote: Prophetic accountability that turns confession into a completed psalm — attached to Psalm 51's superscription.

genealogy.note: The prophet who confronted David over Bath-sheba and Uriah in 2 Samuel 12; his full narrative role belongs to the Samuel index, noted here only for Psalm 51's superscription.

verses.note: Superscription: 'A Psalm of David... when Nathan the prophet came unto him, after he had gone in to Bath-sheba.'

funFacts: Psalm 51 is the Psalter's best-known psalm of personal repentance, directly tied by its own superscription to Nathan's confrontation narrated in 2 Samuel 12:1-13.

characters.name: Doeg the Edomite
characters.perkNote: Named only in a psalm superscription recalling betrayal — a lore-tag attachment to David's tier, not a moral endorsement.

genealogy.note: An Edomite, chief herdsman to Saul (1 Samuel 21:7), whose report to Saul in 1 Samuel 22:9-10 triggered the massacre of the priests at Nob; noted here only for Psalm 52's superscription.

verses.note: Superscription: 'when Doeg the Edomite came and told Saul, and said unto him, David is come to the house of Ahimelech.' The psalm denounces the informant directly: 'Thy tongue deviseth mischiefs.'

funFacts: 1 Samuel 22:18-19 records Doeg personally carried out Saul's order to kill eighty-five priests at Nob after Saul's own guards refused.

characters.name: Cush the Benjamite
characters.perkNote: Occasion-only figure named solely in Psalm 7's superscription.

genealogy.note: Named only in Psalm 7:1's superscription as 'Cush the Benjamite' — he does not appear anywhere in the historical narrative books, and his identity and occasion are otherwise unknown.

verses.note: Superscription: 'Shiggaion of David, which he sang unto the LORD, concerning the words of Cush the Benjamite.'

funFacts: Cush the Benjamite is not mentioned anywhere outside this single psalm superscription; some commentators have speculated 'Cush' was a nickname for a member of Saul's own tribe (Benjamin), but scripture gives no further identification, and this index does not assert one.
